passages.title: Earth today
passages.text: The planet as satellites see it now: land, sea and cloudless colour. Today’s imagery, whatever the date shown: the ancient Earth’s own colours are not known. The imagery shows no sea ice, so today’s (NSIDC, the 1981–2010 mean of March and of September) is laid over it, by the time of year: the north’s ice widest in March and least in September, the south’s the other way round. The time of year is counted in tropical years, so a Julian date long drifted from the seasons still gets its own season. Travelling the years, it is blended towards the ice age’s by how far the sea had fallen. A stand-in for any past year: two maps a year can only sketch the season, and 1981–2010 is neither the Little Ice Age nor today.

passages.title: The planets’ moons
passages.text: Where Mars’s, Jupiter’s and Saturn’s moons are, and what is known of each. Mars’s two moons, Jupiter’s four large ones and Saturn’s eight go round their planets at their true sizes, each painted roughly its colour: each orbit is a mean orbit fitted to JPL’s ephemerides from 1750 to 2200, its angles turning steadily, with the swings a resonance adds (Mimas’s with Tethys, Hyperion’s with Titan). Over those years each moon is within a fifth of a degree of JPL’s place, as seen from its planet, but Mimas (half a degree) and Hyperion (four degrees). Outside them the orbits are carried on at the same rates, which says only roughly where a moon was: centuries away, where Phobos was along its orbit is unknown. Close up, twelve of them wear their missions’ global maps (Galileo and Voyager for Jupiter’s four, Cassini for Saturn’s, Viking for Phobos), each turned to keep the face it keeps to its planet; Deimos and Hyperion, with no map fit to use, keep a colour. Titan, whose ground no eye has seen through its haze, has a Light switch: its ground in near infrared (its usual map), by Cassini’s radar (a preliminary mosaic, with gaps where the radar never looked), and as it looks, all orange haze. What the bar says of each moon (who found it, what it is known for) comes from NASA’s pages on it, its missions’ pages, and the papers behind the findings, at the length its story deserves; what is not settled is said to be so.

passages.title: Sun, Moon and planets
passages.text: Where the Sun, the Moon and the planets were at the moment shown, and the day and night they make. Worked out in your browser: the Sun by Meeus’s formulas and the Moon by ELP/MPP02, both checked against JPL DE441 (the Moon’s mean motion refitted to it); the planets by VSOP87. Clock time is turned into Earth’s turning by ΔT, whose uncertainty grows the further back the date.

passages.title: Eclipses
passages.text: The year’s eclipses, their times and magnitudes, and the Moon’s shadow on Earth. Computed for this site from JPL DE441 with Skyfield. Where on Earth an eclipse was seen depends on ΔT, which is uncertain by minutes to hours in antiquity: the paths shift east or west with it.

passages.title: The Sun close up
passages.text: The Sun’s surface in the light picked, from the surface outward: its spots, its magnetic field, then ever hotter layers above it. Images of 2024, days apart, stitched into one surface: the Sun of the date shown looked different, in ways unknown. The four hotter layers are seen in extreme ultraviolet, each through a filter that passes the light of one kind of atom at one temperature (helium in the chromosphere, iron in the corona). They are named by wavelength in ångströms (Å), a tenth of a nanometre: visible light is about 6,000 Å, these 131 to 304 Å. Earth’s air blocks this light, so only spacecraft see it.

passages.title: Carbon-14 in the air
passages.text: How much carbon-14 the air held each year, as tree rings, corals and cave formations record it: the curve every radiocarbon date is read against. The line is the curve’s Δ14C: the air’s carbon-14 against a modern standard, per mille. IntCal20 for the northern hemisphere, SHCal20 for the southern, picked by where you stand. Living things take in the air’s carbon-14 and, once dead, lose half of it every 5,730 years; a laboratory measures what is left, as a radiocarbon age. Because the air’s carbon-14 rose and fell, that age is read against this curve to find calendar years: where the curve is steep, a narrow range; where it is flat (the Hallstatt plateau, about 800–400 BCE), centuries; where it wiggles, two or more ranges. Miyake events, sudden one-year rises from solar storms, let a tree ring be dated to its year. The curves end in 1950: after it nuclear tests nearly doubled the air’s carbon-14 (the bomb pulse). Under the line, each tick is an eruption the ice cores of Greenland and Antarctica record, as tall as the sulfur it sent into the stratosphere (HolVol, 9500 BCE to 1900 CE): its haze cooled the following summers, which tree rings record as frost rings and narrow rings. The ice cores were lined up with the tree rings by the same Miyake spikes, 774 and 993 CE, which left beryllium-10 in the ice as they left carbon-14 in the wood. Most eruptions are known only from the ice; the strip names those its sources do (Samalas, Tambora). Their dates are good to a few years over the last 2,500 years, to 5–15 years before that, and to about 66 years at 9500 BCE. “How was this dated?” works through two real eruptions: Thera, whose age falls on a plateau and whose date is still debated, and Changbaishan, dated to 946 CE by counting a tree’s rings from the 775 CE spike.

passages.title: Radiocarbon dates
passages.text: Where archaeologists have dated remains by carbon-14: bones, charcoal, seeds, shell, from about 35,000 sites. About 170,000 dates gathered from many regional databases by the p3k14c project. Each is a radiocarbon age, so it is calibrated here, against IntCal20 north of the equator and SHCal20 south of it, and placed at its median calendar age; then counted by 1° square and 250 years, back to 10,550 BCE. The squares are deeper where there are more dates, on a scale against the busiest shown. They show where dates have been measured, not how many people lived: some regions, Europe and North America above all, have been dug and dated far more than others. The database fuzzes its locations to protect the sites, so a square is as close as it goes. Picking a place lists its sites, and “How was a date here found?” carries one of its dates across the curve again.

passages.title: Carbon-14 made in the sky
passages.text: Where cosmic rays make carbon-14 in the air, and how it reaches living things: the clock a radiocarbon date reads. Cosmic rays strike the air high up; neutrons from the shower turn nitrogen-14 into carbon-14. Earth’s magnetic field turns slower rays away, least near the poles, so several times more is made over the poles than over the equator. The rates are Kovaltsov et al.’s model, computed here from their yield function: by their own reckoning about 1.6 atoms per cm² each second on average over 1951–2010. A weaker field or a quieter Sun lets more rays in: with no field, about twice as much. By default the field is that of the moment shown, from the GGF100k model, back 55,000 years: it fell to about a third of today’s in the Laschamp excursion, 41,000 years ago, and models fitted to the excursion alone put it far lower (Korte et al. 2019). The glow is drawn about the spin axis, which the field lines up with when averaged over thousands of years; today it is tilted about 10°. Mixed through the air as carbon dioxide within a few years, carbon-14 enters plants, then animals; the ocean takes it in slowly, so a sea shell reads about 400–600 radiocarbon years older than a plant of the same year (Marine20 against IntCal20, the last 11,000 years). At death the intake stops and half is gone every 5,730 years. After about 50,000 years too little is left to measure. Started from the Sun, the story begins in its core, at about 15 million degrees (Bahcall et al. 2005), where fusion gives off gamma rays; that light takes about 170,000 years to random-walk to the surface (Mitalas & Sills 1992; quick estimates give ten times less, and the energy itself, rather than one photon, takes tens of millions of years, Stix 2003); leaves the surface at 5,772 K (Prša et al. 2016) and reaches Earth in 8 minutes 19 seconds. Chlorophyll absorbs its red light, near 680 nm (Barber 2003), and reflects the green.

passages.title: The Moon and planets close up
passages.text: What the Moon and each planet look like near to: the missions’ own maps of them. Each map is wrapped on the body as published, shrunk for the web, and each planet is turned as it was at the moment shown, by the IAU’s rotation models, the light’s travel time allowed for: the face toward you is the one that faced you then (checked against JPL Horizons). Jupiter’s and Saturn’s turning is that of their interiors (System III): their clouds drift against it, so a cloud feature is not where it was that day. Venus shows its cloud tops as a plain colour, as from space the clouds hide the ground; its Light switch shows the ground beneath instead, as Magellan’s radar mapped it, coloured by height. Mercury’s switch shows MESSENGER’s enhanced colour, which tells its rocks apart, and Jupiter’s sets Hubble’s map of 2024 beside Cassini’s of 2000. Saturn’s map has gaps where Cassini could not see (the poles, and the strip in the rings’ shadow): they are filled with the colour of the nearest latitude imaged. No sharper map of the whole of Saturn has been made: this one is at the camera’s own limit. Its rings are drawn as measured: how much light gets through at each radius from Voyager 2’s watch of a star passing behind them (every 10 km, the C ring to the F ring), and their colour from Cassini’s panorama of their lit side, tied to radius at the edges of the B and A rings. The height maps come with a colour key. USGS publishes none for Mars’s and the Moon’s, so theirs is measured: the map’s colours read against the altimeters’ own heights at the same places (MOLA’s and LOLA’s gridded records), one colour a kilometre, from the sunlit half of each kilometre’s pixels so the shading does not darken it. Venus’s is read off the legend USGS publishes with its map. The enhanced-colour maps (the Moon’s, Mercury’s) colour kinds of rock, not heights: their keys name each kind as its source describes it, with the colour the map gives a place known for it (Mare Tranquillitatis for the seas richest in titanium), read off the map there. Close up, Mercury, Venus (by radar), the Moon and Mars name their largest features, as the IAU names them: the largest first, as many as fit without crowding, more as you zoom in, and only on the day side, where they can be seen. Long, thin features (ridges, scarps, troughs) are left out, as their name would sit on only a part of them.

passages.title: The night sky
passages.text: The stars as seen from the place picked, at the moment shown. Each star carried back along its own motion through space, and the sky turned by precession to the date shown.

passages.title: States and empires (Cliopatria)
passages.text: The borders of states and empires in the year shown, and their names. Borders simplified and split by century for this site. Cliopatria’s latest borders, of 2024, stand for the years since. OpenHistoricalMap draws some borders differently: pick it, or both to compare, in Layers.

passages.title: States and empires (OpenHistoricalMap)
passages.text: The borders of states and empires in the year shown, and their names. Borders simplified and split by century for this site. Cliopatria draws some borders differently: pick it, or both to compare, in Layers.

passages.title: ΔT
passages.text: How far Earth’s turning had fallen behind a uniform clock by the date shown, and how sure that is. It moves where on Earth an eclipse was seen. Splines fitted to ancient and modern observations from 720 BCE to 2015 CE, and a long-term parabola outside them (as Skyfield has them). The ± is an approximate standard error, 0.8 t² seconds for t centuries from 1820, at least a second.

passages.title: Poles, magnetic field, tilt, day and Sun
passages.text: What Earth was like then, beyond its map: where its poles were, its magnetic field, its tilt, the length of its day and the Sun’s brightness. Each fact names its source in its text. The day’s length is read between measurements (corals, a rudist shell, tidal rhythmites), and its ± is the source’s where it gives one. The magnetic field’s reversals of the last 83 million years are GTS 2020’s, as PmagPy carries them; before that, the superchrons, and between them a field reversing too often to draw here. The globe’s poles are the spin axis; magnetic north is marked at the pole a compass pointed to, averaged over thousands of years. Where sources disagree (a much larger Precambrian tilt; the faint young Sun paradox) the text says so.

passages.title: Ways of life
passages.text: How people lived in each region, as archaeologists rated it: foraging, herding, farming, intensive farming, towns. Each region shaded by its most widespread way of life at the rated moment nearest the year shown (ten moments, 10,000 years ago to 1850); mixed where several are as widespread. Region outlines simplified.

passages.title: Named periods
passages.text: The archaeological and historical periods named for the place picked. Periods matched to the country at the place picked by their Wikidata identifiers; each listed with the source that defines it.

passages.title: Ancient genomes
passages.text: Dated ancient DNA, counted by region within 250 years of the year shown. Ancient individuals that pass the resource’s own assessment, counted by 2° cell.

passages.title: Rocks at the surface
passages.text: How old the rocks at the surface are today. World map units, simplified for this site.

passages.title: Impact craters
passages.text: Craters and deposits left by asteroids and comets, and in deep time, where they lay when they struck. Places when they struck reconstructed on the PALEOMAP model by the GPlates Web Service. A crater’s card estimates the impactor’s size from the crater by Collins et al.’s scaling laws, under assumptions it states; “Play the impact” is an illustration, with Chicxulub’s approach from Collins et al. 2020 and the others assumed. “Impacts through time” draws each crater’s place every 5 million years from its strike to today: as a track on a map of today’s coasts (Natural Earth), a picked crater followed by a dot along it, or as a line through a 3D box of longitude, latitude and time. The reconstruction reaches 540 million years back, so older craters start there; craters dated only loosely are drawn faint from the middle of their span.

passages.title: Volcanic eruptions
passages.text: Eruptions dated near the year shown, sized by explosivity.

passages.title: Spacecraft beyond Earth
passages.text: Every craft sent beyond Earth orbit, from Luna 1 in 1959 to today, where it was at the moment shown, and those that set out but never left. The record is Jonathan McDowell’s GCAT: each craft that left Earth orbit (not its rocket stages), with each stretch of its flight about one body, and its landing; NASA NSSDCA’s chronology gives each mission’s objective and outcome, and the craft that set out but never left (failures at launch, probes stranded in Earth orbit). Paths are JPL Horizons’s where it has the craft (about 95), thinned to as few points as draw them within 75,000 km about the Sun, 1,000 km through a flyby, 500 km near Earth; a long stay in orbit is drawn at its world. For the others the path is approximate, drawn amber: each leg as the transfer orbit between where it left and where it arrived, as first planned, not as flown; within about 0.02 AU of Horizons for a direct transfer. A leg to a comet or asteroid, or one that loops back to the world it left, is not drawn.

passages.title: The asteroid belt
passages.text: The main belt’s asteroids at least 100 km across, between Mars and Jupiter, where each was at the moment shown. Which asteroids, their names and their diameters are JPL’s Small-Body Database’s: every one in the main belt it gives as 100 km across or more, some two hundred, from Ceres (939 km) down; the hundreds of thousands smaller are left out. Each is drawn as a dot, the larger ones larger, not to scale: at the scale of the Solar System even Ceres would be far too small to see. Its orbit is a mean orbit about the Sun fitted to JPL Horizons from 1600 to 2500, as the moons’ are: the elements JPL publishes for an asteroid hold only at their epoch, and carried with Kepler’s laws alone they stray tens of degrees in a few centuries, as Jupiter pulls on the asteroids. Fitted, half are within a degree of JPL’s place along their orbits throughout those years, as Ceres and Vesta are (within half a degree), and 169 of the 210 within two. The furthest out, held in step with Jupiter (the Hildas, which go round three times to its two, and Thule, four to its three), are swung by it most: up to 12 degrees off. Each card says how close its own fit came. Outside those years the orbits are carried on at the same rates: where an asteroid is along its orbit is then only roughly known.

passages.title: Planets’ orbits
passages.text: The paths of Earth and the five bright planets around the Sun. Each orbit sampled at 128 points around the date shown.

passages.title: The Earth then
passages.text: Land, sea and mountains as one reconstruction draws them for the moment shown. Elevation grids smoothed to 0.2°, seams repaired, and blended between the maps either side of the moment. The maps put the poles of their time at top and bottom, so “North pole then” and “South pole then” are the map’s own. Period names and dates from the ICS chart. Other reconstructions place the continents differently: turn on Plates to outline Cao et al. 2024’s over this one.

passages.title: How do we know what Earth looked like?
passages.text: The globe is a reconstruction: a model of where land and sea, mountains and shelves were, built from evidence that survives in rocks. Some of it is measured, some inferred, some the map-maker’s judgement. This is what it rests on. Other reconstructions place the continents differently, the more so further back: Cao et al. 2024 (turn on Plates to outline it over this map), Merdith et al. 2021, Müller et al. 2019 (from the Triassic).

passages.title: The ice ages’ Earth
passages.text: Today’s land and sea floor, with the coast at the sea level of the moment and the ice sheets of the time. Sea level from the reconstruction picked, laid on today’s depths (not on the land as it was); ice from PaleoMIST every 2,500 years, with Batchelor et al.’s outlines at their time slices. PaleoMIST's grounded ice stops a little short of the coasts and leaves out the floating ice shelves, so today's ice to the coast (Natural Earth's glaciated areas and Antarctic ice shelves) is drawn under it at every moment: between today and 80,000 years ago Antarctica and Greenland always had at least today's ice. Sea level by Bintanja & van de Wal or by Spratt & Lisiecki: pick whose to follow.

passages.title: Temperature
passages.text: The surface coloured by its temperature, or over the last 800,000 years by its change from today, and each model’s mean. Over the last 800,000 years, Krapp et al. (2021): annual mean temperature on land every 1,000 years, of which the site keeps every other, a statistical emulator of 72 HadCM3 climate-model runs driven by CO₂, Earth’s orbit and the ice sheets, averaged by the site to a 1° grid; the sea and the ice sheets have none and keep their relief colours. Its maps are on today’s geography, so a place can be set beside itself today: by default the colours show that change, blue colder and red warmer; within about a degree of today the land is left uncoloured, so a scale's pale middle is not taken for ice. Further back, maps every 5 million years, packed into images and blended between them. Krapp et al. is a model emulator, not proxy measurements: the ice cores and reconstructions in the boundaries story’s Holocene chapter are the measured side. Its mean is over ice-free land only, and a different land at each moment: at an ice age's height the ice-covered land is left out and the bared shelves come in, so the mean understates the cold (about 4 °C below today at the last glacial maximum, where places by the ice were near 20 °C colder) and cannot be set beside the others' global means. Scotese 2022 and CESM (Li et al. 2023) disagree, at times by several degrees: pick whose to colour by.

passages.title: Sea level
passages.text: Sea level through time, as each reconstruction has it, on a chart. Each reconstruction is drawn side by side; they differ, the more so further back.

passages.title: Plates
passages.text: A second reconstruction’s continents, outlined over the first. Continent outlines reconstructed with pyGPlates in the model’s paleomagnetic frame, drawn as 0.25° masks.

passages.title: Humans
passages.text: Dated finds of our species and its relatives, and where a dispersal model has people settled. Each find is shown with the paper that dates it, and rival dates side by side. The dispersal model is one model’s view, not evidence.

passages.title: Air
passages.text: Carbon dioxide and methane from the ice cores, and carbon dioxide and oxygen from proxies over 540 million years. Proxy estimates scatter widely: each study’s points are shown, by method.

passages.title: Tree of life
passages.text: How the living things on this site are related: one tree from the first cells to our species, the fossil genera on the map hung on it. Open Tree of Life’s synthetic tree, which merges hundreds of published phylogenies and fills the gaps from its taxonomy, trimmed to the backbone down to orders, the site’s fossil genera and our species with its closest relatives. Drawn as a radial tree: the root at the centre, each level further out, each group a wedge as wide as its share of the tips. Branch lengths mean nothing here: the tree says who is related to whom, not when they split. Where no published phylogeny places a taxon, only the taxonomy does: the tree marks those. Some named groups are not one branch in the synthesis (Open Tree calls them broken): many dinosaurs, Tyrannosaurus among them, hang beside the node named Dinosauria rather than under it, so they take the colour of the next group up.

passages.title: Fossils
passages.text: Fossils of four groups of animals, counted by 5 million years and 5°, where they lay then. Places at their age on the PALEOMAP reconstruction.

passages.title: Life through time
passages.text: Each genus of four groups of animals as a line through time, from its first fossil to its last, standing where its fossils lay then and joined to its family and order. The Paleobiology Database’s classification gives each genus its family, order and so on, and its first and last appearance; its finds give where it lay, placed at their age on the PALEOMAP reconstruction and averaged every 5 million years. A family or order starts where and when its oldest member does. The floor is PALEOMAP’s elevation map at the slider’s moment. Footprints, burrows and eggs, which PBDB names apart from the animals that made them, are left out. The classification is a taxonomy, not a dated phylogeny: branch points are drawn at the oldest fossil found, and true splits came earlier. Open Tree of Life’s synthesis, on the tree of life, places some of these genera differently; both are kept.

passages.title: Search
passages.text: The site’s texts found by their words, or by their meaning, each opening the view of the place and time it is about. Every text the site shows is cut into passages, each tied to the bodies, places and years it is about. Words are matched as typed, ranked by BM25. Search by meaning, once turned on, runs a small English model, bge-small-en-v1.5, in your browser: it turns the question into 384 numbers that stand for its meaning, and the passages, turned into numbers the same way beforehand, are ranked by how alike they are; the two lists are then merged. The model and its runtime are downloaded from this site once, about 48 MB; nothing typed leaves the browser. A model of meaning can be wrong: it ranks by likeness, not by truth, so each passage found says where it comes from.

passages.title: Planetary boundaries
passages.text: Why the boundaries sit where they do: global temperature over 800,000 years, through the ice ages to the narrow band it kept for the 10,000 years before industry, the Holocene corridor, and out of it. Then the nine Earth-system processes that keep the planet in a Holocene-like state, each with a boundary to human pressure, and where each control variable stood in the Planetary Health Check 2026: inside its safe operating space, in the zone of increasing risk, or in the high-risk zone. Beside it, the assessment the report compares itself with, Richardson et al. (2023). The temperature chart is this site's own drawing of the four records the report's Figure 1 cites, fetched and checked by the data pipeline: the EPICA Dome C ice core (Antarctic, thinned to 200- and 1,000-year means), the Last Glacial Maximum Reanalysis (median and 95% range of 500 members), PAGES 2k (31-year filtered ensemble) and HadCRUT5 (annual, the latest, perhaps partial, year left out). The global records are set against 1850–1900; the corridor is the range of the reanalysis' medians over the 10,000 years before 1950, computed, not drawn. The values are the report's Table 7.1, typed by hand, for both assessments; each boundary's status in words is the report's own, and the site checks that its drawing agrees with every one. Each wedge reaches from the variable's reference value (0) through its boundary (1) to its high-risk line (2), beyond that eased so the strongest transgressions stay in view; each assessment is drawn against its own boundaries. Ranges (extinction rates, HANPP) and judgements (novel entities, with no numbers past its boundary) are drawn faded past their sure part. The 2023 values are taken as the 2026 report reprints them. The scene and its colours are this site's own, after the report's description of its diagrams. While the Holocene chapter's chart draws, the globe follows it: the ice sheets (PaleoMIST, with Batchelor et al.'s outlines), the coast at the sea level of the time (Bintanja & van de Wal, on NOAA's present-day depths), the sea ice (blended from NSIDC's today towards a PMIP4 model's glacial maximum) and, on land, Krapp et al.'s temperature as the change from today; from 1850, Berkeley Earth's measured temperature of land and sea (the sea's surface water, from HadSST4; the air over sea ice) as 5-year means against 1850–1900. Where a place had too few records in 1850–1900 (about a third of the land, much of it tropical, and two fifths of the sea, away from the ships' tracks), its warming is measured from 1951–1980 and shifted back by how much warmer 1951–1980 was than 1850–1900 in its 15° band of latitude, land and sea apart: some 0.3 to 0.6 °C on land, 0.05 to 0.4 °C at sea. That shift is estimated, the warming since is measured. Inland Antarctica, without records that long, is left plain, as is the sea where the early years have too few records. The ice core is Antarctic temperature, which swings about twice as far as the globe's: it is drawn faint and named, not rescaled. Records disagree on the Holocene's slow trend: the reanalysis drawn (Osman et al. 2021) has it warming gently, where others have it peaking some 6,000 years ago and cooling; the corridor holds either way. Where the two assessments differ, the site shows both rather than choose. Global phosphorus: the 2026 table gives 4.4 Tg/yr, inside the boundary, where 2023 gave 22.6, yet the report's text still calls both nutrient boundaries strongly transgressed and lists no new data for them. Forest cover rose from 60% to 64%, and its boundary from 75% to 78%, through a corrected method, the report says, not forest recovering. Ocean acidification crossed its boundary for the first time in 2026, by a hair (Ω 2.85 against 2.86), with four data products where 2023 had one. Aerosols over South Asia are measured against a boundary proposed in 2026, not yet counted in the global status. On the globe, Krapp et al.'s maps are measured from their own present, which is pre-industrial, and Berkeley Earth's from 1850–1900: close, but not the same reference, so the colours may step slightly at 1850. Land has warmed faster than the sea (some 2 °C against about 1 °C in recent years), so the continents look warmer than the chart's line and the oceans cooler. Before 1850 the sea is left plain: Krapp et al.'s maps cover land only. Within about a degree of the reference the land is left uncoloured. High latitudes have warmed most: since 1951–1980 Arctic land some 2.5 °C, the tropics' about 1.2 °C.

passages.title: Phobos
passages.text: The larger of Mars’s two moons, a lumpy body some 27 km long, scarred by the 9 km crater Stickney. It is closer to its planet than any other moon, about 6,000 km above Mars, and goes round in 7 hours 39 minutes, faster than Mars turns: seen from Mars it rises in the west and sets in the east. Tides are drawing it in by about 1.8 m a century; in some 50 million years it will crash into Mars or break up into a ring. Whether it and Deimos are captured asteroids or the debris of a great impact on Mars is still argued. JAXA’s MMX, launched in October 2026, is to bring a sample of it back to Earth in 2031. Found by Asaph Hall, August 1877.

passages.title: Deimos
passages.text: Mars’s smaller, outer moon, some 15 km long, smoothed by a blanket of dust. It goes round in 30 hours, so from Mars it hangs in the sky for days at a time, a bright star. Found by Asaph Hall, August 1877.

passages.title: Io
passages.text: The most volcanic body in the solar system, with hundreds of active volcanoes, some throwing plumes hundreds of kilometres high; its yellows and reds are sulphur. Jupiter’s tides knead it from within: its orbit is kept out of round by a resonance with Europa and Ganymede (four turns of Io to two of Europa and one of Ganymede), so it is squeezed and released every 42 hours. Its volcanoes were found in Voyager 1’s images in 1979, by Linda Morabito. Found by Galileo Galilei, January 1610.

passages.title: Europa
passages.text: Under a shell of ice lies an ocean of salt water, holding perhaps twice the water of all Earth’s oceans: Galileo’s magnetometer found the field such an ocean would carry. With water, the chemistry its rocky floor could supply, and the energy of Jupiter’s tides, it is among the most promising places to look for life beyond Earth. Its surface is young, few craters, criss-crossed by cracks and ridges. Hubble has seen what may be plumes of water vapour, not yet confirmed. NASA’s Europa Clipper, launched in October 2024, is to arrive in 2030 and fly past it dozens of times. Found by Galileo Galilei, January 1610.

passages.title: Ganymede
passages.text: The largest moon in the solar system, larger than Mercury, and the only moon known to make its own magnetic field (Galileo, 1996). Hubble watched its aurorae rock less than they would over solid ground, a sign of a salty ocean beneath the ice. ESA’s JUICE, launched in 2023, is to orbit it from 2034: the first spacecraft to orbit a moon other than our own. Found by Galileo Galilei, January 1610.

passages.title: Callisto
passages.text: The most heavily cratered body known: its surface has hardly changed in some four billion years. Its largest scar, the Valhalla basin, is a bright centre some 600 km across, ringed out to some 1,500 km from it. Galileo’s magnetometer hinted at an ocean deep below its ice, as at Europa and Ganymede, less certainly. Found by Galileo Galilei, January 1610.

passages.title: Mimas
passages.text: The smallest and innermost of Saturn’s major moons, its face marked by the 130 km crater Herschel, a third of its width across, which makes it look like the Death Star. Its pull sets the inner edge of the Cassini Division, the widest gap in Saturn’s rings. In 2024 its slight wobble and orbit were found to fit a young ocean under its ice, likely less than 25 million years old: a surprise on a moon that looks long dead. Found by William Herschel, 1789.

passages.title: Enceladus
passages.text: The whitest body in the solar system. In 2005 Cassini found jets of water vapour and ice shooting from four long cracks near its south pole, the “tiger stripes”, from a global ocean under the ice; they feed Saturn’s E ring. Flying through the jets, Cassini tasted salts, organic molecules, molecular hydrogen, a sign of hot water reacting with rock at the ocean floor as at Earth’s hydrothermal vents, and phosphates. With liquid water, energy and these ingredients, it is one of the best places in the solar system to look for life. Found by William Herschel, 1789.

passages.title: Tethys
passages.text: Almost all water ice. The crater Odysseus spans some 400 km, nearly two fifths of its width, and the canyon Ithaca Chasma runs some 2,000 km, from near one pole to the other. Found by Giovanni Domenico Cassini, 1684.

passages.title: Dione
passages.text: Ice over rock, its trailing side streaked by bright cliffs of ice hundreds of metres high, cracks in its crust. Cassini found a trace of an oxygen atmosphere, and its shape and gravity suggest an ocean deep beneath the ice, less certainly than at Enceladus. Found by Giovanni Domenico Cassini, 1684.

passages.title: Rhea
passages.text: Saturn’s second-largest moon, a cold ball of ice and some rock. In 2010 Cassini found a tenuous atmosphere of oxygen and carbon dioxide around it. Found by Giovanni Domenico Cassini, 1672.

passages.title: Titan
passages.text: Larger than Mercury, and the only moon with a thick atmosphere: mostly nitrogen, its pressure at the ground half again Earth’s, hazy orange with hydrocarbons. Methane plays the part water does on Earth: it rains, carves rivers, and fills lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane near the poles, Kraken Mare and Ligeia Mare the largest. Titan is the only place besides Earth known to have standing liquid on its surface. Its dunes are grains of hydrocarbons; beneath its ice crust is likely an ocean of water. ESA’s Huygens probe landed there on 14 January 2005, the farthest landing yet; NASA’s Dragonfly, a rotorcraft, is to launch in 2028 and fly from place to place studying its chemistry, the kind that may have led to life on Earth. Found by Christiaan Huygens, March 1655.

passages.title: Hyperion
passages.text: Not round but a tumbling, sponge-like lump some 410 km long, so porous that much of it is empty space; it turns chaotically, with no steady day. Found by William and George Bond, and William Lassell, September 1848.

passages.title: Iapetus
passages.text: Two-faced: the side it leads with is as dark as coal, the other as bright as snow. Cassini, who found it, could see it on one side of Saturn but not the other, and guessed as much. Around its middle runs a ridge of mountains some 10 km high, giving it the look of a walnut. Found by Giovanni Domenico Cassini, October 1671.

passages.title: The Ugarit eclipse
passages.text: A clay tablet from the city of Ugarit on the Syrian coast describes the day the Sun was put to shame. It is one of the oldest records proposed to describe a solar eclipse. Both the reading of the tablet and the date are disputed; 1375 BCE May 3 has also been proposed. With this site's ΔT model, Ugarit sees about 94% of the Sun covered, not totality, even allowing for ΔT's uncertainty.
passages.cite: Tablet KTU 1.78; date proposed by de Jong & van Soldt (1989)

passages.title: The eclipse proposed for the Odyssey
passages.text: As Odysseus returns to Ithaca, the seer Theoclymenus says the Sun has perished from the sky. Astronomers have proposed that the line remembers a real total eclipse, in 1178 BCE. Most classicists read the line as poetry, not a record; the proposed date rests on other astronomical hints in the poem, which are themselves disputed.
passages.cite: Homer, Odyssey 20.356–357; date proposed by Schoch (1926) and by Baikouzis & Magnasco (2008, PNAS 105, 8823)

passages.title: The Assyrian eclipse
passages.text: The Assyrian eponym list notes a solar eclipse in the month Simanu in the year of the official Bur-Sagale. Matching it to this eclipse anchors Assyrian chronology, and through it much of ancient Near Eastern history.

passages.title: The oldest eclipse in Ptolemy's Almagest
passages.text: Ptolemy used three lunar eclipses observed in Babylon in the first two years of King Mardokempad (Merodach-baladan II). This, in 721 BCE, is the oldest dated observation in the Almagest.

passages.title: The total eclipse in the Spring and Autumn Annals
passages.text: The Chunqiu, the chronicle of the state of Lu, records a solar eclipse in the third year of Duke Huan and says it was total, one of the earliest records of a total eclipse. Whether totality reached the capital depends on ΔT within its uncertainty, which is why records like this one help historians and astronomers pin down ΔT.
passages.cite: Chunqiu (Spring and Autumn Annals), Duke Huan year 3

passages.title: The Babylonian eclipse of Nabopolassar's fifth year
passages.text: Ptolemy's Almagest quotes Babylonian observations of a lunar eclipse in the fifth year of King Nabopolassar. Because Ptolemy also gives the reign, this record helps tie Babylonian regnal years to absolute dates.

passages.title: The eclipse of Thales
passages.text: Herodotus writes that day turned to night during a battle between the Lydians and the Medes, ending a six-year war, and that Thales of Miletus had foretold it. With this site's ΔT model, the path of totality crosses Asia Minor from the Aegean to northern Syria; where the battle took place is not known. At the Halys, the usual guess, it was partial: the path of totality passed further south. This is the usual identification, but the battle's place and year are uncertain, and whether Thales could have predicted it is doubted.

passages.title: The lunar eclipse of Cambyses' seventh year
passages.text: Ptolemy cites a Babylonian observation of a lunar eclipse in the seventh year of the Persian king Cambyses; a cuneiform tablet from the same year also records it.
passages.cite: Ptolemy, Almagest V.14; tablet Strm. Kambys. 400

passages.title: The eclipse in the first summer of the Peloponnesian War
passages.text: Thucydides writes that at a new moon, after midday, the Sun was eclipsed, took the shape of a crescent so that some stars appeared, and then became full again.
passages.cite: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 2.28

passages.title: The eclipse at Syracuse
passages.text: Thucydides tells how a lunar eclipse made the Athenian commander Nicias delay his army's retreat from Syracuse, with disastrous consequences.
passages.cite: Thucydides, History of the Peloponnesian War 7.50

passages.title: The eclipse before Gaugamela
passages.text: A total lunar eclipse eleven days before Alexander the Great defeated Darius III at Gaugamela; ancient historians and Babylonian astronomical diaries both mention it.
passages.cite: Arrian, Anabasis 3.7; Plutarch, Alexander 31; Babylonian astronomical diaries

passages.title: Agathocles' eclipse
passages.text: As Agathocles of Syracuse sailed for Africa, slipping past a Carthaginian blockade, day turned to night and the stars came out, Diodorus writes. The eclipse is a classic check on how fast Earth's rotation has slowed.

passages.title: The lunar eclipse before Herod's death
passages.text: Josephus mentions a lunar eclipse shortly before the death of Herod the Great. This partial eclipse is the traditional identification. Several eclipses have been proposed, notably the total lunar eclipse of 1 BCE January 10; the choice shifts the date of Herod's death.

passages.title: The alternative eclipse for Herod's death
passages.text: A total lunar eclipse on the night of 9–10 January 1 BCE (Jerusalem time), proposed as an alternative to 4 BCE for the eclipse Josephus mentions before Herod's death. One of several proposals; see also 4 BCE March 13.

passages.title: The eclipse before Louis the Pious died
passages.text: The emperor Louis the Pious saw a great eclipse in May 840; his biographer links it to his death six weeks later.
passages.cite: The Astronomer, Life of the Emperor Louis, ch. 62

passages.title: The eclipse of the Battle of Stiklestad
passages.text: Snorri Sturluson writes that the Sun went dark during the battle in which King Olaf II of Norway was killed. An eclipse crossed Norway that summer, on 31 August. The sagas date the battle to 29 July, a month before the eclipse; the darkening may have been moved to the battle in the telling, or the battle's date is wrong.
passages.cite: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla, Saga of Olaf the Saint ch. 227

passages.title: King Henry's eclipse
passages.text: As Henry I of England set out for Normandy, the Sun was eclipsed and stars appeared; chroniclers took it as an omen, and he never returned to England.
passages.cite: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle (Peterborough), 1135 [for 1133]; William of Malmesbury, Historia Novella

passages.title: Columbus's eclipse
passages.text: Stranded on Jamaica, Christopher Columbus used an almanac's prediction of this total lunar eclipse, on the evening of 29 February 1504 local time, to persuade the local Taíno people to keep supplying his crew.
passages.cite: Ferdinand Columbus, The Life of the Admiral; Regiomontanus's Ephemerides

passages.title: Halley's eclipse
passages.text: Edmond Halley published a map predicting the path of this total eclipse across England and asked observers to report what they saw, an early example of crowd-sourced science.

passages.title: The eclipse that revealed helium
passages.text: Observing this total eclipse from India, Jules Janssen saw a bright yellow line in the solar spectrum that turned out to belong to a new element, helium.

passages.title: Eddington's eclipse
passages.text: Expeditions to Príncipe and Sobral measured how the Sun's gravity bent starlight during this total eclipse, the first test of Einstein's general relativity.

passages.title: The last total eclipse of the millennium
passages.text: A total eclipse crossed Europe from Cornwall to Romania and on to India, watched by hundreds of millions.

passages.title: The Great American Eclipse
passages.text: The first total eclipse to cross the contiguous United States from coast to coast since 1918.

passages.title: The 2024 North American eclipse
passages.text: A total eclipse from Mexico's Pacific coast across Texas, the Great Lakes and Newfoundland.

passages.title: The 2026 eclipse over Iceland and Spain
passages.text: The first total eclipse visible from mainland Europe since 1999, crossing Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain near sunset.

passages.title: The great Egyptian eclipse
passages.text: One of the longest total eclipses of the century, with more than six minutes of totality near Luxor.
